opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a complicated feeling, and a good one in the end.

When Sora came out and people started connecting it back to the Diffusion Transformer work, the DiT paper Bill Peebles and I did, my first reaction was happiness for Bill. He was a student doing an internship, we were exploring something that felt fairly simple at the time: can we take the transformer, which had worked so well in language, and use it as the backbone for diffusion models instead of the U-Net everyone had been using? It wasn't a flashy idea. We were just trying to understand scaling behavior, whether more compute gives you cleaner, better images in a predictable way. Seeing him take that line of thinking and push it to that scale at OpenAI was really meaningful.

The second feeling was more reflective. It reminded me what academic research is actually for. In universities we don't have tens of thousands of GPUs. We can't train the biggest model. But we can ask a clean question, run a careful experiment, and publish it openly so anyone can build on it. If that small seed ends up inside a system that changes how people think about video generation, that's the system working the way it should. Open research flowing into industry and coming back is healthy.

And to be honest, there's a third feeling, a bit of pressure. It made me ask: what's the next thing academia should be working on that industry *isn't* yet? Not just chasing the same scaling curve with fewer resources, but asking deeper questions about visual representation, about world models, about how vision connects to language and reasoning. That's where I think a university lab can still be a few steps ahead.

So mostly I felt proud, a little humbled, and motivated. It's encouraging to know that a paper written in a fairly modest setting can still matter.

r001.rationale: The candidate says university research can ask clear questions, run careful experiments, and publish work that others build on, and that this modest academic paper meaningfully influenced a major OpenAI system.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a very strange and humbling feeling. When we were doing the DiT work at NYU with Bill Peebles, we were just trying to answer a fairly simple research question: can you replace the U-Net backbone in diffusion models with a plain transformer, and does it scale the way transformers scale elsewhere? It was a small academic project. We didn't have huge compute, and the paper was actually rejected at first. So when Sora came out and people started pointing to DiT as one of the foundations behind it, my first reaction wasn't pride, it was more like disbelief.

But after that initial surprise, I think there were two things I took from it. The first is that it validated something I believe deeply about academic research: our job is not to build the final product. Our job is to find the right questions, do the careful ablations, and show a clean signal, something like "this scales, and here's the evidence." Industry labs have the resources to take that signal and push it to the extreme. That division of labor is actually healthy. We shouldn't be trying to compete with OpenAI on compute; we should be trying to be one step ahead on ideas.

The second thing is that it made me more aware of a certain tension. A lot of the follow-up work happens behind closed doors now. So you see the result, you see the demo, but you can't see the details, and you can't build on them directly. That's a real loss for the field. It made me more committed to keeping our work open, releasing code and models, because that openness is exactly what allowed that connection to happen in the first place.

And of course, on a personal level, for my students it was a huge motivation. It showed them that a university lab, with limited resources, can still shape where the whole field goes. That's probably the part I value most.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the experience showed students that a university lab with limited resources can still shape the direction of the field.

astra-6.text: It meant a lot to me. When you’re doing research at university, you’re often focused on a very specific question, and you don’t know how far that work will travel. Seeing it inspire researchers at OpenAI was encouraging. It made the impact of research feel tangible—that something you explored could become a starting point for someone else to take further.

Seeing researchers at OpenAI pick it up and build on it made me feel that the work had value beyond the original paper. That’s one of the most rewarding parts of research for me: you put an idea out there, and other people take it in directions you hadn’t imagined.
